questions.q: What does an adapter do?
questions.explain: Your services depend on SmsSender; the adapter turns those calls into the vendor SDK's calls and turns the vendor's answers back into SmsResult.
options: It adds logging and retries to an object
It implements the interface your code expects by calling a different interface (usually third-party), translating in both directions
It creates objects of the right class
It stores objects in a database

questions.q: Which list covers what an SMS adapter must translate?
questions.explain: The login outage came from two missed translations: the number format and a failure reported inside a successful response. An adapter that skips any of the four leaks the vendor into your code.
options: Only the method name
The method name and the API key
The request shape, data formats (such as phone numbers), the response shape, and errors
Only errors, since the rest is the same for every vendor

questions.q: A vendor's SDK does not throw for an invalid number; it resolves with status: "InvalidPhoneNumber" inside the response. What should the adapter do?
questions.explain: Callers only understand your result type. Mapping the vendor's in-band failure into it is the adapter's job; retrying a permanent failure would never succeed.
options: Nothing; no exception means success
Throw a generic Error for every non-success status
Read the status and return { ok: false, reason: "invalid_number" }, so callers see the failure in the shape they already handle
Retry until the status is "Success"

questions.q: Why does the lesson normalise phone numbers in one shared nigerianE164 function before each adapter converts to its vendor's format?
questions.explain: Validation is shop knowledge (DRY), while "no plus sign" or "plus sign" is vendor knowledge. Keeping them apart means a new vendor needs only its own small conversion.
options: Because adapters may not contain regular expressions
So there is one definition of a valid number; each adapter only converts from the canonical form to its vendor's format
Because the vendors require it
To make the adapters slower

questions.q: What is an anti-corruption layer?
questions.explain: If a vendor's response type appears in a service's signature, the layer has a hole. Everything inside the layer speaks your domain's language.
options: A security filter that blocks SQL injection
A layer of adapters that keeps an external system's vocabulary, types and quirks from spreading into your own code
A layer that encrypts data at rest
A test that detects corrupted files

questions.q: How does a facade differ from an adapter?
questions.explain: A checkout() in front of pricing, payment and stock is a facade. termiiSender is an adapter. Wrappers around big SDKs are often a bit of both.
options: They are the same pattern
A facade puts one simple interface in front of a complicated subsystem; an adapter converts one interface into another that callers expect
A facade is only for user interfaces
An adapter always wraps several objects, a facade exactly one

questions.q: Why run one contract test against every SMS adapter?
questions.explain: This is Liskov substitution in practice. The contract would have caught the login outage before the vendor switch shipped.
options: To measure which vendor is faster
All adapters promise the same behaviour through the same interface, so one suite proves each one keeps the promise (valid number delivered, invalid number reported, network error mapped)
Because TypeScript cannot check adapters
To avoid writing an interface

questions.q: What makes an object a decorator?
questions.explain: Because the interface is the same, callers cannot tell a decorated sender from a plain one, and decorators can be stacked. TypeScript's @decorator syntax is a separate language feature.
options: It is written with the @ syntax
It implements the same interface as the object it wraps, forwards calls to it, and adds behaviour before or after
It extends the class it decorates
It changes the interface of the wrapped object

questions.q: Which SMS failure should a retry decorator retry?
questions.explain: Only transient failures can succeed on a second try. Invalid numbers and rejections are permanent; retrying wastes time and money.
options: invalid_number
rejected (the vendor blocked the sender id)
unavailable (the connection dropped)
All of them, three times each

questions.q: A retry after a dropped connection sends the message again, but the provider had actually received the first request. When is that acceptable?
questions.explain: A dropped connection does not tell you whether the request arrived. A duplicate login code is harmless; a duplicate charge is not.
options: Always; duplicates are the provider's problem
Only when repeating the operation is harmless (idempotent), or when the provider supports an idempotency key that makes it ignore the duplicate
Never; network errors must not be retried
Only for payments

questions.q: Why do production retries wait longer between attempts (backoff) and add some randomness (jitter)?
questions.explain: Immediate, synchronised retries can turn a short outage into a longer one. Backoff spreads the load over time; jitter spreads it across clients.
options: To make logs easier to read
To give a struggling service time to recover, and to stop thousands of clients from retrying at exactly the same moments
Because JavaScript timers are inaccurate
To use up the request's time budget

questions.q: withLogging(withRetry(sender)) versus withRetry(withLogging(sender)), for a send that fails twice and then succeeds. Which is true?
questions.explain: The outermost decorator sees one call in and one result out. A decorator inside the retry sees every attempt.
options: Both log three lines
The first logs one line (the final result); the second logs one line per attempt
The first logs three lines; the second logs one
The order of decorators never matters

questions.q: Why is the wait function injected into withRetry instead of calling setTimeout directly?
questions.explain: Time is part of the outside world, like the network. Injecting it (a wait function, a clock) makes timing behaviour testable and deterministic.
options: Because setTimeout does not work in async functions
So tests run instantly and can check exactly which waits happened (100 ms, then 200 ms), while production passes a real sleep
So the retry can run in parallel
To make the decorator a singleton

questions.q: Why does the logging decorator write +234****567 instead of the full phone number?
questions.explain: A logging decorator sees every argument of every call. Masking belongs in it, so no call site can forget.
options: To save disk space
Logs are copied, shipped and kept for a long time; full phone numbers there are personal data that should not be exposed
Because the vendor requires masked numbers
Because the full number is not available to the decorator

questions.q: A caching decorator is put in front of getAccountSummary(token) and caches by the URL path only. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: Anything that depends on who is asking must include the caller in the key, or not be cached at all.
options: Nothing; caching is always safe
The first user's summary is cached and served to everyone who requests the same path: a data leak
The cache fills up too slowly
The TTL becomes zero

questions.q: A proxy and a decorator can look identical in code. What is the difference?
questions.explain: Lazy creation, permission checks and forwarding over the network are access control. Logging and retries are added behaviour. The names help readers understand why the wrapper exists.
options: A proxy always uses JavaScript's built-in Proxy
The intent: a decorator adds behaviour; a proxy controls access to the real object (whether, when or how it is reached)
A decorator changes the interface, a proxy does not
A proxy can only wrap classes

questions.q: A lazy proxy does if (real === undefined) real = await create(). Two requests arrive at the same moment. What happens, and what is the fix?
questions.explain: The check and the assignment are separated by an await, which lets the other request run in between. A promise exists immediately, so the second caller finds it.
options: Nothing goes wrong; JavaScript is single-threaded
Both see undefined before the first await finishes and create two objects. Cache the promise (real ??= create()) so both wait for the same creation
The second request throws
The fix is to make create synchronous

questions.q: The lazy proxy caches the creation promise. The first creation fails because the font files are missing. What should happen next time?
questions.explain: A cached rejection turns a temporary problem into a permanent one until restart. Remove it in a catch and rethrow.
options: Return the same rejected promise forever
Clear the cached promise on failure, so a later call can try again (for example after the files are restored)
Create a new object on every call from now on
Return undefined

questions.q: A protection proxy checks role === "admin" before exportAllCustomers. When does it protect nothing?
questions.explain: An access check that can be walked around is decoration. The raw service must never be handed out; only the guarded one is.
options: When the user is an admin
When other code can still import or receive the real, unwrapped service and call it directly
When the method is async
When the proxy is created per user

questions.q: Which of these is a remote proxy?
questions.explain: The caller uses a normal interface; the proxy hides serialization and the network. That convenience also hides latency and partial failure, which callers must still handle.
options: A cache in front of a slow function
An RPC client object whose methods look local but send each call to another service over the network
A retry decorator
An in-memory repository

questions.q: Why does calling a method through new Proxy(account, {}) fail when the method reads a #private field?
questions.explain: Private fields belong to real instances only. This is one reason plain wrapper objects are usually clearer than the built-in Proxy for these patterns.
options: Proxies cannot forward method calls
The method runs with this set to the proxy, which is not an instance of the class and so has no private field
Private fields are removed when an object is proxied
It does not fail

questions.q: What problem does a repository solve?
questions.explain: When the total column was renamed, four files broke. With a repository, one file changes and services never see column names.
options: It makes SQL run faster
SQL and row mapping for one kind of domain object are scattered across services; a repository puts them behind one collection-like interface in domain terms
It replaces the database
It creates database tables

questions.q: What is wrong with a generic Repository<T> that offers findWhere(filter: any)?
questions.explain: The point of a repository is to hide storage. A method that takes a storage-shaped filter hides nothing.
options: Generics are not allowed in repositories
It leaks the query language into every service, so storage details spread again; methods should be named after domain questions like findOverdue(now)
It is too slow
Nothing, it is the recommended design

questions.q: An order and its lines are always saved and loaded together. How many repositories should they have?
questions.explain: Two repositories invite saving an order without its lines. One repository keeps the aggregate consistent.
options: Two: one per table
One: a repository per aggregate (objects that change together), so an order is always saved with its lines
None; use raw SQL
One per line item

questions.q: A repository loads 50 orders, then runs one query per order to load its lines. What is this called, and why is it a problem?
questions.explain: Load related data in one query (a join) or one query per kind (all lines for these 50 orders).
options: Lazy loading; it is always fine
The N+1 query problem: 51 round trips to the database instead of one or two, which is slow under load
A transaction; it locks the table
A cache miss; it cannot be fixed

questions.q: Why does the PostgreSQL repository cast total_kobo::int, and why does the contract check that amounts are numbers?
questions.explain: Only a contract run against the real database sees what the driver actually returns. The in-memory version would never show it.
options: Because PostgreSQL cannot store integers
The pg driver returns bigint columns as strings, so without the cast services would receive text and total + fee would join strings
Because JavaScript has no integer type
To make the query faster

questions.q: Why is the repository's save written as an upsert (INSERT … ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE)?
questions.explain: The contract checks it: after saving ORD-2 twice, there is one ORD-2 with the new status.
options: Upserts are faster than inserts
So saving the same order again updates it instead of failing or duplicating, which matches the collection-like meaning of save and makes it safe to repeat
Because PostgreSQL requires it
To delete old orders

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The SDK does not throw, so the first version reports success. Only reading the status inside the response reveals the failure. That reading belongs in the adapter.
options: failed failed: InvalidPhoneNumber
sent failed: InvalidPhoneNumber
sent sent
failed sent

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Spaces and dashes are removed first. The third number has only ten digits and no leading 0 or country code, so it matches no pattern.
options: [ undefined, '+2348031234567', undefined ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first call fails with a transient error, the second succeeds, and the loop stops as soon as the result is ok. Three attempts is a maximum, not a target.
options: true 3
true 2
false 1
false 3

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The outermost decorator runs first on the way in and last on the way out, like layers of an onion. Middleware pipelines behave the same way.
options: inner in, outer in, outer out, inner out
outer in, inner in, inner out, outer out
outer in, outer out, inner in, inner out
inner in, inner out, outer in, outer out

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: First call: miss (1). At 999 the entry (expires at 1000) is still fresh: hit. At 1000, 1000 > 1000 is false, so it has expired: miss (2). A different pair is a different key: miss (3).

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first call stores the promise synchronously, before any await, so the other two find it and wait for the same creation.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Called on the real instance, the method works. Called through the proxy, this is the proxy, which has no #kobo, so reading it throws a TypeError.
options:
250000
true

250000
false

true
true

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The guard works, but the unwrapped service is still reachable and refunds anyway. A protection proxy only protects if the raw object is never handed out.
options: forbidden forbidden
forbidden refunded ORD-9
refunded ORD-9 refunded ORD-9
refunded ORD-9 forbidden

questions.q: A driver returned a bigint column as a string. What does this print?
questions.explain: The as unknown as number lie hides the string from TypeScript, so + joins text. The mapping in the repository is where a string must be converted, and a contract test against the real driver is how you find out.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Promise.race settles with the first promise to settle. The hanging promise never does, so the timer wins; an already resolved promise wins over a 10 ms timer.
options:
timed out
late

timed out
sent

sent
sent
It never finishes

questions.q: Write vendorSender(sdk), an adapter implementing SmsSender for the SDK below. It must pass the number without the leading +, return { ok: true, messageId: ref } when accepted, { ok: false, reason: "invalid_number" } when error === "BAD_MSISDN", and { ok: false, reason: "unavailable" } when the SDK throws. The program should print true false invalid_number false unavailable.
questions.explain: The adapter translates the number format, the response and the exception. Services only ever see SmsResult.

questions.q: Write withRetry(sender, attempts): call sender.send, and while the result is { ok: false, reason: "unavailable" } and attempts remain, call it again. Other failures must not be retried. The program should print true 3 then invalid_number 1.
questions.explain: Two transient failures, then success on the third attempt. A permanent failure returns at once: retrying it could never help.

questions.q: Write withLogging(sender, log) that calls the wrapped sender and then logs "<masked>: <status>", where the masked number keeps the first 4 and last 3 characters with **** between, and the status is ok or the failure reason. The program should print [ '+234****567: ok' ].
questions.explain: The decorator has the same interface as the sender, returns the same result, and keeps the full number out of the logs.

questions.q: Write withCache(source, ttl, clock) for a price(sku) source: return the cached value while clock.now() is before the entry's expiry, otherwise call the source and store the new value until now + ttl. The program should print 1 2.
questions.explain: Two reads within the TTL cost one call. At exactly the expiry time the entry is stale, so a second call is made. The injected clock makes that edge testable without waiting.

questions.q: Write lazy(create): it returns a function get() that starts create() on the first call and returns the same promise to every caller. The program should print 1 true.
questions.explain: Storing the promise, not the finished object, means the second caller joins the creation already in progress instead of starting another.

questions.q: Write guardedPayouts(user, payouts), a protection proxy: list() is allowed for everyone, approve(id) only for users with role "finance"; others get new Error("forbidden"). The program should print 2, forbidden, approved PO-1.
questions.explain: The proxy has the same interface and decides per call whether to let it through. It only protects if code outside receives the guarded object, never payouts itself.

questions.q: Write a MemoryCustomerRepository with save(customer) (stores e-mails in lower case, replacing any customer with the same id) and findByEmail(email) (case-insensitive, returns the customer or undefined). The program should print Ada Obi, 1, undefined.
questions.explain: Saving the same id twice replaces instead of duplicating, and e-mail lookups ignore case. Those rules would go into a contract test shared with the database version.

questions.q: Write toOrder(row) that maps a database row { id, customer_email, total_kobo, placed_at } (where total_kobo arrives as a string) into { id, email, totalKobo, placedAt } with totalKobo as a number and placedAt as a Date. The program should print 1591575 2026-03-01T10:00:00.000Z.
questions.explain: The mapping from storage shape to domain shape lives in one function inside the repository. Services get camelCase names, numbers and dates, and never see a column name.
